title: Letter IV
focus: the meeting of two ambitious men

teacherSummary.text: Trapped in ice, Walton's crew sees a giant figure on a dog sled, and the next morning rescues a frozen, exhausted stranger: Victor Frankenstein. Victor recovers slowly, becomes Walton's friend, and, hearing of Walton's ambition, agrees to tell his own story as a warning.

vocabulary.definition: To settle or draw up the heads or terms of an agreement, as in chapters or articles
vocabulary.context: Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: One who guards, protects, watches over, or has the care of, some person or thing
vocabulary.context: You have been tutored and refined by books and retirement from the world, and you are, therefore, somewhat fastidious; but this only renders you the more fit to appreciate the extraordinary merits of this wonderful man.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: An optical instrument used in viewing distant objects, as the heavenly bodies
vocabulary.context: We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being raw
vocabulary.context: He manifested the greatest eagerness to be upon deck, to watch for the sledge which had before appeared; but I have persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Coming or happening as a consequence or result
vocabulary.context: He entered attentively into all my arguments in favour of my eventual success, and into every minute detail of the measures I had taken to secure it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To throw rays of light upon
vocabulary.context: Even now, as I commence my task, his full-toned voice swells in my ears; his lustrous eyes dwell on me with all their melancholy sweetness; I see his thin hand raised in animation, while the lineaments of his face are irradiated by the soul within.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Having a disposition to do good
vocabulary.context: “And yet you rescued me from a strange and perilous situation; you have benevolently restored me to life.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Yet his manners are so conciliating and gentle, that the sailors are all interested in him, although they have had very little communication with him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: But he is generally melancholy and despairing; and sometimes he gnashes his teeth, as if impatient of the weight of woes that oppresses him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: To flow in a small, gentle stream
vocabulary.context: At first I perceived that he tried to suppress his emotion; he placed his hands before his eyes; and my voice quivered and failed me, as I beheld tears trickle fast from between his fingers—a groan burst from his heaving breast.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: The frame (Walton) now opens into Victor's narrative, a 'story within a story' structure called a nested or frame narrative.

significance: Victor's warning, 'Learn from me,' makes the whole novel a cautionary tale addressed to Walton and to the reader.
discussionQuestions: Victor says he will tell his story so Walton may learn from it. What lesson do you predict?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Letter IV,” how does Shelley show the meeting of two ambitious men? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter IV develops the idea of the meeting of two ambitious men. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Letter IV to complicate the reader's understanding of the meeting of two ambitious men. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the meeting of two ambitious men responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter IV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the meeting of two ambitious men. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

options: An optical instrument used in viewing distant objects, as the heavenly bodies
To flow in a small, gentle stream

satQuestions.passage: About two o’clock the mist cleared away, and we beheld, stretched out in every direction, vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end. Some of my comrades groaned, and my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts, when a strange sight suddenly attracted our attention, and diverted our solicitude from our own situation. We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile: a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge, and guided the dogs. We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes, until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Letter IV”?
options: The meeting of two ambitious men

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Victor says he will tell his story so Walton may learn from it. What lesson do you predict? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include capitulated, tutored, telescopes, rawness, eventual. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To settle or draw up the heads or terms of an agreement, as in chapters or articles.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The frame (Walton) now opens into Victor's narrative, a 'story within a story' structure called a nested or frame narrative. Now, why does this chapter matter? Victor's warning, 'Learn from me,' makes the whole novel a cautionary tale addressed to Walton and to the reader. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Point of view.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot foreshadowing, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
